sections.heading: Coming before your greatness
sections.text: God over all things, your greatness is beyond what we can measure. Your name is worthy of the highest praise, and your glory is higher than the heavens. Angels serve you, and countless creatures stand before you. In your holy presence, we see how small we are. We do not come to you because we have earned your attention. We come because we need you, and because you have invited needy sinners to come.
theological_themes: God is sovereign, majestic, and worthy of worship.
Human beings approach God with humility, not entitlement.
God's invitation gives sinners courage to draw near.

scripture_references.connection: This verse grounds the prayer's confession that God's greatness cannot be fully searched out or measured by us.
The passage invites believers to come near to God for mercy and help, not because they are worthy in themselves, but because God has opened the way through Christ.

sections.heading: Why we dare to ask for mercy
sections.text: Father, please look on us with mercy. Our sin gives us no claim on you, but our need drives us to you. Your promises give us hope. Our wounded and stubborn hearts need your help. Jesus our Mediator brings us near. And when we see how you have welcomed and forgiven others, we are encouraged to ask you to receive us too.
theological_themes: God's mercy is the only safe ground for sinners.
Christ is the Mediator who brings people to God.
God's past mercy to others encourages present faith.

scripture_references.connection: This passage identifies Jesus as the one Mediator between God and humanity, which supports the prayer's confidence that we come to God through him.
The tax collector's plea for mercy shows the posture of sinners who do not justify themselves but cast themselves on God's compassion.

sections.heading: Seeing sin clearly and finding life in Jesus
sections.text: Show us the truth about our sin—its guilt, its damage, and the way it stains us. Do not let us make peace with what separates us from you. Give us faith to trust Jesus, and as we trust him, give us the life that is found in him alone.
theological_themes: Sin brings guilt and inner corruption.
God must awaken true conviction and repentance.
Life is received through faith in Jesus Christ.

scripture_references.connection: This passage holds together the seriousness of sin and the gift of eternal life in Christ, matching the section's movement from conviction to life in Jesus.
John states that believing in Jesus leads to life in his name, directly supporting the prayer's request for faith that receives life in Christ.

sections.heading: Trusting you in grief and staying faithful
sections.text: Teach us to know Christ even in suffering, without pretending pain is easy or good in itself. When grief comes through people, events, or losses, help us see that nothing is outside your wise rule. Keep us from bitterness, and keep us from using sorrow as a reason to stop obeying you. Even when we are weeping, help us keep sowing what is good. Even when life keeps changing, set our hearts on the lasting city you have promised. Stay with us to the end of our journey, so that we may honor you in dying as well as in living.
theological_themes: Believers share in Christ's sufferings without adding to his saving work.
God's providence rules over grief without making evil good or excusing wrongdoing.
Sorrow should not stop faithful obedience.
Christians live toward the eternal city and seek to glorify God in life and death.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks of knowing Christ and sharing in his sufferings, which illuminates the prayer's request to enter into Christ's sufferings as fellowship with him.
This passage teaches that God works in all things for the good of those who love him, supporting trust in providence even when grief comes through painful circumstances.
The psalm's image of sowing in tears directly supports the prayer's request that weeping not keep us from faithful labor and hope.
This verse points believers beyond the instability of the present world toward the city to come, matching the prayer's longing for what abides.

sections.heading: Committing this night to you
sections.text: Thank you for keeping us today, for providing what we needed, and for every mercy we noticed and every mercy we missed. You are the keeper of our souls, so we place ourselves, our bodies, our minds, our homes, and all we have into your hands tonight. Guard us from evil. Spare us from sickness and fear, as far as it pleases you. Let nothing dark or terrifying rule our thoughts. Give us clear consciences, clean hearts, and peaceful sleep.
theological_themes: God preserves and provides for his people.
Believers entrust their whole selves to God at the close of the day.
Peaceful sleep is received as a gift from God's care, not as something we control.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm describes the Lord as the keeper of his people in their going out and coming in, fitting the prayer's entrusting of life, possessions, and safety to God.
David connects peaceful sleep with the Lord's protection, which directly supports the request for safe and restful sleep.
Peter calls suffering believers to entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good, which fits the prayer's commitment of all we are to God.

sections.heading: Joining the worship of heaven
sections.text: And now, while we sleep and the heavenly host never grows tired, we join their praise. To the Lamb on the throne—Jesus Christ our Savior—be blessing, honor, glory, and power forever and ever. Amen.
theological_themes: Christ the Lamb is enthroned and worthy of worship.
Earthly prayer joins the worship already being offered in heaven.
The final word of the day belongs to the glory of Christ.

scripture_references.connection: This scene of countless heavenly beings praising the Lamb closely grounds the prayer's closing act of joining heaven's worship of Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original request that no sickness come near could be read as a guaranteed promise of health. The adaptation keeps it as a humble request for protection, qualified by trust in God's will, rather than a claim that believers will not suffer illness.

The original phrase about seeing God's hand in the instruments of grief requires care. The adaptation preserves robust providence while avoiding the implication that God approves of evil actions or that human agents are excused.

The request to enter into Christ's sufferings can be misunderstood as contributing to Christ's atoning work. The adaptation frames it as fellowship with Christ in suffering, not participation in redemption as co-atonement.

The original's language of being 'less than nothing' is a strong humility expression. The adaptation renders it as seeing our smallness before God's holy presence without denying human dignity as God's image-bearers.
significant_interpretive_choices: The prayer's movement was preserved as evening worship: adoration, humble approach, mercy and conviction, suffering under providence, nightly commitment, and heavenly praise.
The phrase 'Thy acceptance of others moves us' was interpreted as encouragement drawn from God's mercy to other sinners, rather than comparison or envy.
The line 'Let not our weeping hinder sowing; nor sorrow, duty' was rendered concretely as continuing to do good and obey God even while grieving.
The 'abiding city' was interpreted in light of the New Testament hope of the city to come, not as any earthly institution or cultural project.
